notes:
I've written notes for most verses from 1 to 24, but some of the requested material is missing. My search and fetch limits ran out before I could reach the Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Reformed (ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org), Methodist, Orthodox, netbible.org and bibleodyssey.org pages. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage. Where I report a tradition's view, I say whose description it is. Often it comes from a commentator outside that tradition.

**Luke 22:1–24 notes**

**1. The traditional reading, verse by verse**

v. 1: Passover and Unleavened Bread were strictly two separate feasts: Passover on Nisan 14–15, then Unleavened Bread on Nisan 15–21. Luke uses the names interchangeably. Arnold Fruchtenbaum notes that by Jesus' day they were kept as one eight-day festival. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary
- Commentators disagree on the day. Fruchtenbaum puts vv. 1–6 on Tuesday, while MacArthur places the events in Luke 22:1-6 on Wednesday. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary
- Guzik points out that the timing mattered: Jerusalem was packed with crowds hoping for the Messiah, including many from Galilee who respected Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Darrell Bock (quoted by Precept Austin) sees irony here: a festival celebrating life becomes the setting for a plot to kill the one who brings life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

v. 2: In Guzik's words, the leaders did not fear God, but they did fear the people. They were not afraid to kill the Son of God; they just had to find a politically smart way to do it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- J.C. Ryle (quoted by Precept Austin) calls this the start of Luke's account of Christ's sufferings, the part of the Gospels that matters most. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

v. 3: Guzik says Satan prompted Judas and perhaps guided him. That does not lessen Judas's guilt, because Satan worked with Judas's will, not against it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- On "Iscariot," Guzik gives two explanations. It may mean "from Kerioth," which would make Judas the only Judean among Galileans. Or it may be linked to *sicarius* ("assassin") and the Zealots. He finds no biblical support for the theory that Judas had a noble motive. He suggests Judas may have followed Jesus for selfish reasons and turned on Him when Jesus proved not to be the Messiah he wanted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Matthew Henry: Whoever betrays Christ, or his truths or ways, it is Satan that puts them upon it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

v. 4: Henry notes the leaders needed an insider who knew where Jesus went to be alone, and that Judas approached them himself. He warns that treacherous "pretended friends" may harm Christ's kingdom more than open enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

v. 5: Guzik uses Matthew 26:14–16 to show that Judas asked for a price, which points to simple greed. He also asks why Satan would push events toward the cross that defeated him. His suggestion is that Satan's hatred, and his own self-deception, got the better of him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 6: Guzik sees God using Judas's wicked acts to advance His plan. Fear of the crowd had led the leaders to delay, but Judas's treachery let it happen at the appointed time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Henry guesses that Judas quietly asked Peter and John where Jesus would be, and that they did not suspect him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

v. 7: Guzik says Passover remembered the central act of redemption in the Old Testament, and Jesus was about to give a new centre of redemption, remembered in a new meal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Spurgeon notes that Jesus kept the ordinances of the old covenant for as long as it lasted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke

vv. 7–13 (dating the meal): The Synoptic Gospels present a Passover meal, but John seems to place the crucifixion on Passover itself. Guzik cites Leon Morris's suggestion that two calendars were in use, and Adam Clarke's similar view. He also notes that no lamb is mentioned, perhaps to stress that Jesus Himself was the sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Morris calls this one of the most difficult questions in New Testament interpretation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

v. 8: Henry suggests Jesus may have gone to preach in the temple that morning while Peter and John made the arrangements. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

v. 10: Guzik says a man carrying a water jar would stand out, because this was usually women's work and men carried liquids in skins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 11: Guzik sees secrecy here: Jesus did not want Judas to betray Him before His last talk with the disciples. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 15: Guzik says Jesus had now reached the main reason He came, to set up a new covenant based on His own sacrifice. In his words, This was not the beginning of the end; it was the beginning of the beginning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Charles Simeon has a sermon on vv. 14–16. https://www.preceptaustin.org/charles-simeon-sermons-on-luke

vv. 17–18: Guzik explains that Jesus took a cup both before and after the bread. That was normal, since a Passover meal had four ceremonial cups. He links "until the kingdom of God comes" to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 19: Guzik says Jesus did not give the usual Passover explanations of the foods. He reinterpreted them in Himself, so the focus moved from Egypt to His own sin-bearing suffering. The meal is for remembering and for fellowship with Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Precept Austin reads "for you" (Greek *huper*) as substitution: His sinless body given in place of ours. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary
- Gill says "given for you" means given as an offering for sin in our place. "This do" means eating in remembrance of His love and of His body offered for us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-19.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-19.html
- Constable: "in remembrance of me" encouraged the disciples to focus on the person of Jesus Christ and not just the benefits of His death for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-19.html
- The Light of Israel commentary sees the unleavened bread as a picture of Jesus' sinless life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-19.html
- Utley notes that no lamb is mentioned. He sees the meal as a new exodus from sin, the new covenant of Jeremiah 31. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22

v. 20: Guzik says only the God-man could set up a new covenant, sealed in blood as the old one was (Exodus 24:8). Its content is forgiveness, God's law written on the heart, and closeness to God (Jeremiah 31:33–34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- The Geneva Study Bible: Christ establishes his new covenant and his communication with us by new symbols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-19.htm

v. 21: Guzik says this seems to place Judas at the table when the bread and cup were shared, but adds that Bible students debate it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 22: Guzik says Psalm 41:9 foretold the betrayal, yet Judas could never claim he helped by fulfilling prophecy. He stays fully accountable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Henry says Christ was not forced into His sufferings but went to them willingly, and God's plan does not reduce Judas's sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Simeon preached on this verse under the title "The Circumstances of Our Lord's Death Fore-ordained." https://www.preceptaustin.org/charles-simeon-sermons-on-luke

v. 23: Guzik notes that Judas kept his secret well; none of the others suspected him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Precept Austin says Luke compresses three questions from the other Gospels: the disciples' "Surely not I?", Judas's hypocritical version of it, and John's whispered "Lord, who is it?" https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

v. 24: Spurgeon finds the timing of the quarrel astonishing, with their Master going to be crucified for them. He asks whether the same rivalry exists among us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Henry sees these early contests for rank as a sad forecast of later struggles for supremacy in the churches. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

**2. Where Protestant traditions differ**

vv. 19–20, "This is my body": This is the main dividing line. Guzik admits the words have caused great controversy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- **Summary from the ESV Study Bible notes:** Lutherans believe Christ's literal body and blood are present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine. Some Anglicans speak of a "real presence." Most other Protestants believe that the body and blood of Christ are not literally, physically present in the elements of the meal, but that Christ is present symbolically. Most would also add that Christ is present spiritually with and in those who receive the elements in faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/tools/urlReWrites/esvStudyBibleNotesHandler.cfm?shortname=luk&chapter=22&a=995046
- **Lutheran (described by Guzik, not a Lutheran source):** Guzik uses the label "consubstantiation," a term Lutherans themselves usually reject. He tells how, at Marburg, Luther insisted on Christ's words "this is my body" and wrote them on the table. For Luther it was a matter of simply believing what Christ said. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- **Reformed and Zwinglian (described by Guzik):** Calvin taught that Christ's presence is real but spiritual, not physical. Zwingli taught that the bread and wine are meaningful symbols. Zwingli compared the words with "I am the vine" and "I am the door." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- **Puritan, Matthew Poole (quoted by Guzik):** Since "the cup" plainly stands for the wine, Poole says he cannot see why the figure should not be admitted in "this is my body" too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- **Symbolic reading in an older commentary on Bible Hub (the author isn't named in what I saw):** "This is my body" means a representation of His body, just as the lamb was called "the passover." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-19.htm
- **Guzik's own middle position:** The bread and cup are not *mere* symbols but powerful pictures to take part in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

v. 22, God's plan and human responsibility: The sources I read all agree here. Spurgeon (Baptist) says God's decree does not lessen human guilt, since Judas acted freely. He urges readers to believe firmly in Divine predestination without doubting human responsibility. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- I found no Wesleyan or Arminian source for this verse, so I cannot report a contrasting view.

**3. Other views**

vv. 17–20, the shorter and longer text: Some manuscripts end at 19a. In that shorter text the cup comes before the bread, matching 1 Corinthians 10:16 and the *Didache*. The longer text has the order found in Matthew, Mark and 1 Corinthians 11. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22
- A bible.org study says the shorter text was commonly thought original until the 1950s, and the debate is not settled. Nearly all Greek manuscripts, including p75, support the longer text, while the shorter one rests mainly on Codex D and some Latin and Syriac witnesses. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-examination-key-texts-discussion
- The same study says those who prefer the shorter text often think the longer one does not fit Luke's theology, and deny that the passage teaches substitutionary (vicarious) atonement. https://bible.org/book/export/html/1000
- The Expositor's Greek Testament notes that vv. 19b–20 closely resemble Paul's wording in 1 Corinthians 11. Westcott and Hort used that resemblance as an argument against the verses being original. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/luke-22.html

vv. 19–20, Catholic reading: Catholics believe the bread and wine actually become Christ's body and blood (transubstantiation). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- A catholic.com article cites the Council of Trent: by "Do this in commemoration of me," Christ made the apostles priests to offer His body and blood. It argues that the Greek word for "do" can mean "offer" a sacrifice, as in the Greek Old Testament. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/did-jesus-make-the-apostles-priests-at-the-last-supper
- A second catholic.com article argues that "remembrance" (*anamnesis*) has sacrificial overtones. It also points to the present tense in "given" and "poured out." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/evidence-christ-offered-the-last-supper-as-a-sacrifice
- Catholic.com also says the cross was "once for all," and that "do this" tells the apostles to continue the sacrifice of the Mass. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/sacrifice-of-the-mass

**Not found:** I didn't reach verse comments on vv. 9, 12–14 and 16, any Orthodox reading (oca.org), any netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes, or any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace material, so those are left out.
